# sources/test-tools/syzkaller/pkg/report/testdata/linux/report/499

Purpose: Linux reporter parse fixture for syzkaller. It encodes the expected parsed title `<none>`, expected type `<none>`, alternate titles `none`, corrupted flag `N`, and panicked flag `N`. The source is a static kernel-console transcript, not executable test code; its job is to pin how the Linux reporter recognizes non-crash Qualcomm MDSS boot/probe noise fixture. It has no explicit REPORT block, so the parser derives the report from the console transcript and expected headers.

Important APIs, types, and functions: this file is consumed by `pkg/report/report_test.go` through `testParseImpl`, `Reporter.ContainsCrash`, `Reporter.Parse`, and `Reporter.ParseFrom`. It exercises Linux reporter pattern tables and title extraction in `linux.go`, generic report shaping in `report.go`, and crash-type mapping through `pkg/report/crash.TitleToType`. Parser-relevant functions and symbols in the log include mdss_mdp_pipe_addr_setup, mdss_mdp_parse_dt_handler, mdss_smmu_probe, mdss_dsi_get_dt_vreg_data. Diagnostic tokens visible in the complete fixture include no crash-token markers.

Control flow: the test harness enumerates `pkg/report/testdata/linux/report`, reads expectation headers until the blank line or `REPORT:` marker, and feeds the remaining bytes to a Linux `Reporter`. For this fixture, `ContainsCrash` must return false, `Parse` must not manufacture a report, and `ParseFrom` must not rediscover a crash from benign boot/probe output. The log-specific flow is: only informational mdss_mdp, mdss_smmu, mdss_dsi, IOMMU, and device-tree property errors; no TITLE/TYPE header and no crash markers. There are 19 source lines; exact report-body comparison is `no`.

State and persistence behavior: all persistent state lives in this text file: header expectations, alternate titles, crash transcript bytes, and any explicit report body. During tests, state is transient parser output: crash start/end offsets, selected title, alternate titles, crash type, corruption/panic flags, guilty-file hints, and trimmed report bytes. The fixture performs no filesystem, network, device, or kernel mutation; it models those kernel-side events only as immutable input text.

Dependencies and integration points: the fixture integrates with syzkaller's Linux report recognizer, stack-frame skip lists, sanitizer parsers, lockdep/warning/hung-task detectors, panic handling, corruption handling, and report-boundary logic. Product-level consumers are crash deduplication, dashboard grouping, repro triage, maintainers' signal routing, and automated bisection. Because the source lives under `testdata/linux/report`, its filename is intentionally opaque; the headers and transcript are the behavioral contract.

Risks and edge cases: ContainsCrash must stay false despite words such as panic in xlog_status and error messages from display probe. More generally, regressions can come from overfitting to timestamps, CPU/task prefixes, architecture-specific syscall wrappers, compiler suffixes such as `.cold` or `.constprop`, repeated helper frames, panic-on-warn trailers, allocation/free stacks, or noisy subsystem messages preceding the crash. Reports flagged as corrupted must remain conservative about title specificity, while non-crash logs must not be promoted just because they contain alarming words.

Test signals: a passing parser run treats this fixture as non-crashing input: no title, no type, no alternate titles, corrupted `N`, panicked `N`, and no report-body comparison. It must keep the transcript benign, avoid helper-only titles, preserve non-panic/non-corruption semantics, and produce stable negative results across `ContainsCrash`, `Parse`, and `ParseFrom`.
